title: Neural Networks Introduction
tagline: Layered networks of artificial neurons that learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data.

sections.content:
In 2012, a neural network called AlexNet entered the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge and reduced the error rate by nearly 11 percentage points in a single year — a margin that had taken the entire previous decade to accumulate using traditional computer vision. That moment is often called the **deep learning revolution**, and it reshaped artificial intelligence, robotics, medicine, and software engineering almost overnight.

A **neural network** is a computational graph of **neurons** connected by **weights**. Loosely inspired by biological brains, each artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, passes the result through a non-linear **activation function**, and forwards the output to the next layer. Stack enough such layers and the network can approximate virtually any measurable function — a theoretical guarantee called the **Universal Approximation Theorem**. In practice this means: given enough data and compute, a deep network can learn to recognise faces, translate languages, play Go at superhuman level, or predict protein folding structures.

The central idea that distinguishes neural networks from classical machine learning is **end-to-end representation learning**. Instead of hand-crafting features — edge detectors, frequency filters, n-gram counts — you feed raw data directly (pixels, audio samples, characters) and the network discovers its own internal representations during training. Early layers learn to detect low-level patterns (edges, short phonemes, character n-grams); middle layers combine them into mid-level abstractions (textures, syllables, words); later layers recognise high-level concepts (objects, intents, semantics). This learned hierarchy is the engine of modern AI.

In this chapter we will build a complete mental model of neural networks from the neuron upward: the mathematics of a single neuron, the role of activation functions, how layers stack into architectures, the training loop of forward pass and backpropagation, and the vocabulary you need to read modern ML papers and codebases. Along the way we will implement a working network from scratch in plain JavaScript, with no library dependencies, to make the mechanics concrete.

sections.title: A Relay Race of Specialist Filters
sections.content:
Imagine you need to identify whether a photograph contains a dog. Rather than trying to do it yourself in one glance, you hire a large team of specialists arranged in successive rows — each row can only see the row in front of it.

The **first row** looks at tiny 3×3 pixel patches scattered across the image. Each specialist in this row reports a simple judgment: 'I see a diagonal line here,' or 'I see a sharp colour boundary here,' or 'I see a uniform blob of brown.' They cannot see the whole picture — only their small patch. They pass their numerical verdicts forward.

The **second row** receives summaries from the first and looks for combinations: 'a curved edge next to a uniform blob might be an ear,' or 'two parallel edges close together might be a nose.' They synthesise local patterns into parts.

The **third and fourth rows** look for part combinations: ear shapes plus snout shapes plus eye shapes cluster into 'dog face.' By the final row, one specialist outputs a single number close to 1.0 — 'this is almost certainly a dog.'

Each specialist is a **neuron**. The rows are **layers**. The numerical verdicts flowing between rows are **activations**. The crucial insight: nobody told any specialist what to look for. They **learned** their detection criteria entirely from seeing millions of labelled photographs and adjusting whenever their group's final answer was wrong. That collective, distributed self-organisation is deep learning.

sections.title: The Single Neuron: Mathematics from First Principles
sections.content:
A single artificial neuron performs a deceptively simple computation. Given a vector of inputs **x** = [x₁, x₂, …, xₙ], the neuron computes:

`z = w₁·x₁ + w₂·x₂ + … + wₙ·xₙ + b`

which is the **dot product** `w · x` plus a **bias** `b`. This produces a scalar `z` called the **pre-activation** or **logit**. Then the neuron applies a non-linear **activation function** f to get its output:

`a = f(z)`

The weights `w` determine how strongly each input contributes. A large positive weight means 'this input strongly pushes the neuron toward firing.' A large negative weight means 'this input suppresses the neuron.' A weight near zero means the corresponding input is largely ignored. The bias `b` shifts the entire activation threshold independently of the inputs — it is the intercept term in a linear model.

**Why the dot product?** Because it is a measure of alignment between the weight vector and the input vector. When the input pattern strongly matches what the weight vector 'expects,' the dot product is large and positive, causing high activation. This is exactly how a template matcher works: the neuron activates when its input resembles its weight template.

**Why the bias?** Without a bias, every decision boundary must pass through the origin of input space. The bias frees the neuron to position its decision boundary anywhere in space, dramatically expanding expressiveness.

During training, **both weights and biases are adjusted** by gradient descent to minimise the prediction error. A typical network has millions of parameters — all of them weights and biases.

    S --> F["f(z) activation"]

sections.title: Activation Functions: Why Non-Linearity Is Everything
sections.content:
Activation functions are the source of a neural network's expressive power. Without them, composing multiple linear layers simply produces another linear transformation — regardless of how many layers you stack. Mathematically: `W3(W2(W1·x))` = `(W3·W2·W1)·x` = `W_combined·x`. You can always fold any number of weight matrices into a single equivalent matrix. Three layers without activations is no more powerful than one layer.

Activation functions break this collapse by introducing **non-linearity** at every neuron. The combination of many non-linear transformations allows the network to carve input space into arbitrarily complex regions — any shape of decision boundary, any non-linear relationship between inputs and outputs.

**ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)**: `f(x) = max(0, x)`. The single most widely used activation. Its derivative is 0 for x < 0 and 1 for x > 0, which is both cheap to compute and avoids the **vanishing gradient** problem that afflicts sigmoid and tanh for large inputs. The drawback is **dying ReLU**: if a neuron's pre-activation is always negative (e.g., after a large negative gradient update), it outputs zero forever and contributes nothing to training. Variants like **Leaky ReLU** (`max(0.01x, x)`) and **GELU** (Gaussian Error Linear Unit, used in GPT-family models) address this.

**Sigmoid**: `f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x))`. Maps any input to (0, 1), making it ideal for **binary classification output layers** where you need a probability. Its derivative peaks at 0.25 and approaches 0 for large `|x|` — causing vanishing gradients in deep networks when used in hidden layers. Rarely used in hidden layers today.

**Tanh (Hyperbolic Tangent)**: `f(x) = (eˣ − e^(−x)) / (eˣ + e^(−x))`. Maps to (−1, 1) and is **zero-centered** — unlike sigmoid, its output averages near zero, which tends to produce more balanced gradient magnitudes. Used in recurrent neural networks (RNNs/LSTMs) for gating mechanisms. Still suffers vanishing gradients at saturation.

**Softmax**: Not a pointwise function but a vector function: `softmax(x)ᵢ = exp(xᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(xⱼ)`. Converts a vector of raw scores (logits) into a **probability distribution** that sums to exactly 1. Used exclusively on the **output layer** of multi-class classifiers. Each output value is the model's estimated probability for one class.

**GELU / Swish**: Smooth, non-monotonic alternatives to ReLU used in Transformers and modern LLMs. They allow small negative values through (weighted by a sigmoid-like gate), which provides richer gradient flow.

sections.title: Layers and Architectures: Stacking Neurons into Networks
sections.content:
A **layer** is a collection of neurons that all receive the same inputs and whose outputs all feed into the same next layer. Every connection between neuron i in layer l and neuron j in layer l+1 has its own weight w_{ij}. The full set of connections between two layers is compactly represented as a **weight matrix** W, enabling the entire layer computation to be expressed as a single matrix multiplication: `A = f(W · X + b)`.

**Input layer**: Not really a layer of neurons — just the raw feature vector fed into the network. If you are classifying 28×28 grayscale images (like MNIST handwritten digits), the input layer has 784 values (one per pixel). No computation happens here.

**Hidden layers**: One or more layers of neurons between input and output. These are where representation learning happens. In a **feedforward** (fully-connected, or dense) network, every neuron in one hidden layer connects to every neuron in the next. A network with two or more hidden layers is called a **deep** neural network — hence the term 'deep learning.'

**Output layer**: Produces the final prediction. Its activation function is chosen based on the task: sigmoid for binary classification, softmax for multi-class classification, linear (no activation) for regression.

**How many layers and neurons?** A two-layer network (one hidden layer) is theoretically sufficient to approximate any function, per the Universal Approximation Theorem. But in practice, **depth is more efficient than width**: a deeper narrow network often learns better representations with fewer total parameters than a shallower wide one. ResNet-50 (image classification) uses 50 layers. GPT-4 uses 96 Transformer layers. A typical student project might use 2-4 layers.

**Parameter count**: For a dense layer with `n_in` inputs and `n_out` neurons, there are `n_in × n_out` weights plus `n_out` biases = `n_in × n_out + n_out` total parameters. A 784→256→128→10 MNIST network has 784×256 + 256 + 256×128 + 128 + 128×10 + 10 = 234,634 parameters — all learned from data.

sections.title: The Training Loop: Forward Pass, Loss, and Backpropagation
sections.content:
Training a neural network is a cycle of four repeated operations.

**Step 1 — Forward Pass**: Feed a batch of training examples through the network from input to output. Each layer applies its weights and activation to produce activations, which flow to the next layer. The final layer outputs predictions `y_hat`. This is pure function evaluation — no gradient computation yet.

**Step 2 — Compute the Loss**: Compare the network's predictions `y_hat` to the true labels `y` using a **loss function** (also called a cost or objective function). The loss is a scalar measuring how wrong the network is.
- **Mean Squared Error (MSE)**: `L = mean((y_hat - y)²)` — used for regression.
- **Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE)**: `L = -mean(y·log(y_hat) + (1-y)·log(1-y_hat))` — used for binary classification.
- **Categorical Cross-Entropy**: `L = -mean(Σ y_k·log(y_hat_k))` — used with softmax for multi-class.

**Step 3 — Backpropagation**: This is the core innovation that made deep learning practical. Backprop computes the **gradient of the loss with respect to every weight** in the network. It works by applying the **chain rule of calculus** layer by layer, starting from the output and propagating backward to the input.

Intuitively: if the output prediction was too high and the output neuron's pre-activation was positive, we need to decrease the weights feeding into that neuron. But those weights are determined partly by the previous layer's activations, which are determined by weights before that — the gradient must be **chained** all the way back. The chain rule makes this tractable: `dL/dW₁ = dL/da₂ · da₂/dz₂ · dz₂/da₁ · da₁/dz₁ · dz₁/dW₁`. Each factor is a local gradient computed at that layer, and the full gradient is their product.

**Step 4 — Gradient Descent Update**: Once gradients are computed, every weight is updated:
`W ← W − lr · dL/dW`
where `lr` is the **learning rate** — a hyperparameter controlling step size. Too large an lr causes unstable training (the loss bounces or diverges). Too small causes painfully slow convergence. The **Adam optimiser** (Adaptive Moment Estimation) maintains a moving average of gradients and their squares to adapt the learning rate per parameter, and is the practical default for almost all architectures.

This four-step cycle runs on **mini-batches** (typically 32–512 examples at a time) rather than the full dataset, making it **stochastic gradient descent (SGD)**. One full pass over the dataset is called an **epoch**. Typical training runs thousands of epochs on millions of examples.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: This is a complete, runnable neural network with no imports. Key implementation decisions: (1) Small random initialisation — if all weights start equal, every neuron computes the same gradient and learns identically, wasting capacity. (2) The gradient `dZ2 = yHat - y` is the beautiful result of differentiating binary cross-entropy composed with sigmoid — they cancel each other out algebraically, leaving this clean expression. (3) The chain rule appears explicitly: `dA1 = W2 * dZ2` (error propagated back through weights), then `dZ1 = dA1 * sigmoid'(z1)` (scaled by local derivative of activation). (4) XOR requires non-linearity — a straight line cannot separate (0,1) and (1,0) from (0,0) and (1,1) in 2D space. The hidden layer creates a non-linear boundary.

sections.title: Why Backpropagation Works: The Chain Rule Intuition
sections.content:
Backpropagation is often presented as mysterious, but it is just systematic application of a rule from first-year calculus: **the chain rule**. If `y = f(g(x))`, then `dy/dx = f'(g(x)) · g'(x)`. The derivative of a composition is the product of derivatives of each piece.

A neural network is a composition of many functions:
`L = loss(softmax(W₃ · ReLU(W₂ · ReLU(W₁ · x + b₁) + b₂) + b₃))`

To find `dL/dW₁`, we must differentiate through all the functions wrapping W₁. The chain rule says we multiply derivatives together: the derivative of the loss with respect to the softmax output, times the derivative of the softmax, times the derivative of W₃'s multiplication, times ReLU's derivative, and so on all the way back to W₁.

The key computational insight is **reuse**. When computing `dL/dW₃`, we calculate an intermediate value `dL/d(softmax_output)`. When computing `dL/dW₂`, we need that same quantity again, plus the derivative through W₃. Rather than recomputing from scratch, backprop caches these intermediate derivatives and **propagates them backwards**, each layer using the gradient passed from the layer ahead of it. This is why the algorithm is efficient: each parameter's gradient requires only a constant amount of work once the backward pass reaches its layer.

Without backprop, computing the gradient for a network with millions of parameters would require either symbolic differentiation (exponentially expensive) or numerical finite differences (O(n) forward passes, one per parameter — impractical at scale). Backprop is O(n) in both time and space — the same order of complexity as the forward pass itself. This is the algorithmic breakthrough that enabled modern deep learning.

**Vanishing and exploding gradients**: When gradients flow through many layers, they are multiplied together at each step. If the local gradients are consistently less than 1 (as with saturated sigmoid neurons), the product shrinks exponentially toward zero — **vanishing gradient** — and early layers stop learning. If gradients are consistently greater than 1, the product explodes. This is why ReLU (gradient exactly 1 for positive inputs) was revolutionary: it provides a gradient highway through deep networks without saturation.

    O -->|"dL/da2"| H2["Hidden Layer 2"]
    H2 -->|"dL/da1"| H1["Hidden Layer 1"]
    H1 -->|"dL/dW1"| W["Weight Update"]

sections.title: Loss Functions: Measuring What the Network Gets Wrong
sections.content:
The loss function is the network's objective — the single number it is trying to minimise. Choosing the right loss function is as important as choosing the right architecture.

**Mean Squared Error (MSE)**: `L = (1/n) Σ (y_hat_i - y_i)²`. Used for **regression** tasks where the target is a continuous value (predicting house price, forecasting temperature). Squaring the error penalises large errors disproportionately. The gradient is simple: `dL/d(y_hat) = 2(y_hat - y) / n`.

**Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE)**: `L = -(1/n) Σ [y·log(y_hat) + (1-y)·log(1-y_hat)]`. Used for **binary classification** paired with a sigmoid output. Derived from maximum likelihood estimation of a Bernoulli distribution. When the true label is 1, the loss is `-log(y_hat)` — large when y_hat is near 0, zero when y_hat is exactly 1. This asymmetric pressure forces the network to be confident about correct predictions.

**Categorical Cross-Entropy**: `L = -(1/n) Σᵢ Σₖ y_ik · log(y_hat_ik)`. Used for **multi-class classification** with a softmax output. Only the log probability of the true class contributes to the loss; other classes' probabilities matter only indirectly through the softmax normalisation.

**The connection to information theory**: Cross-entropy measures the average number of bits needed to encode the true distribution using the model's predicted distribution. Minimising cross-entropy is equivalent to maximising the likelihood of the true labels under the model — it has deep probabilistic foundations, not just an engineering choice.

**Regularisation terms**: In practice the loss is often augmented with a regularisation penalty. **L2 regularisation** (weight decay) adds `λ Σ w²` to the loss, penalising large weights and reducing overfitting. **L1 regularisation** adds `λ Σ |w|`, which tends to produce sparse weights. Both are just additional gradient terms that the optimizer handles automatically.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three loss functions, each with their analytical gradients. Notice the pattern: every loss paired with its natural output activation (MSE+linear, BCE+sigmoid, CCE+softmax) produces clean, stable gradients. This is not coincidence — these pairings arise from maximum likelihood estimation in statistics. The softmax gradient `probs - one_hot` is particularly elegant: it simply subtracts 1 from the true class's probability, pushing the network to increase confidence in the correct class.

sections.title: Regularisation: Fighting Overfitting
sections.content:
A neural network with millions of parameters can memorise its training data perfectly — producing zero training loss while failing completely on new data. This is **overfitting**: the model learns the noise and idiosyncrasies of its training set instead of the underlying pattern. Detecting overfitting requires a held-out **validation set** that the network never trains on; a widening gap between training loss and validation loss is the signature.

**Dropout**: During each forward pass of training, randomly zero out a fraction (typically 20–50%) of neuron activations in each layer. This forces the network to not rely on any single neuron — every neuron must contribute robustly knowing it might be dropped. At inference time, dropout is disabled and weights are scaled by the keep probability. Conceptually, dropout trains an **ensemble of exponentially many sub-networks** simultaneously, averaging their predictions at inference.

**L2 Regularisation (Weight Decay)**: Adds `λ·‖W‖²` to the loss, penalising large weights. The gradient is `λ·W`, which effectively pushes all weights toward zero unless they have strong gradient evidence to be large. This discourages the network from relying too heavily on any single feature.

**Early Stopping**: Monitor validation loss during training. When it stops improving for a fixed number of epochs (the **patience** hyperparameter), stop training and revert to the checkpoint with best validation performance. This is the simplest regulariser and often the most effective in practice.

**Batch Normalisation**: Not strictly regularisation, but has regularising effects. After a layer's linear transformation, normalise the activations to have mean 0 and variance 1 across the mini-batch, then apply learned scale and shift parameters. This stabilises training (reduces sensitivity to weight initialisation and learning rate), speeds convergence, and acts as a form of noise injection that reduces overfitting.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    OV["Overfitting detected\ntrain loss low, val loss high"]
    OV --> D["Dropout\nrandom neuron zeroing"]
    OV --> L2["L2 Regularisation\npenalise large weights"]
    OV --> ES["Early Stopping\ncheckpoint best val"]
    OV --> BN["Batch Norm\nstabilise activations"]
    OV --> DA["Data Augmentation\nmore diverse training examples"]
sections.caption: Overfitting remedies. In practice, combine dropout + weight decay + early stopping for most architectures. Data augmentation is the highest-leverage remedy when more labelled data is unavailable.

sections.title: Architecture Zoo: Beyond Dense Layers
sections.content:
Feedforward (dense) networks are the foundation, but modern deep learning uses specialised layer types tailored to data structure.

**Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)**: Designed for spatially structured data (images, audio spectrograms). A convolutional layer applies a small **filter** (e.g., 3×3 kernel) to every position in the input by sliding it across, computing dot products. The same filter weights are reused at every position — **weight sharing** — reducing parameters dramatically. A 28×28 image dense-connected to 256 hidden neurons needs 200,704 weights; a 3×3 convolution producing 32 feature maps needs only 3×3×32 = 288 weights. CNNs also respect **translation equivariance**: an edge in the top-left and an edge in the bottom-right produce the same filter response, which is exactly what you want for object detection.

**Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) / LSTMs**: Designed for sequential data (text, time series, audio). An RNN maintains a **hidden state** `h_t` that is updated at each time step: `h_t = tanh(W·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b)`. This allows the network to carry information across arbitrarily long sequences. **Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)** cells add gating mechanisms (input gate, forget gate, output gate) that allow selective reading, writing, and erasing of the hidden state, solving the vanishing gradient problem for long sequences.

**Attention and Transformers**: The architecture behind GPT, BERT, and all modern large language models. Rather than processing sequences step-by-step (like RNNs), attention computes a **weighted sum of all positions simultaneously**: for each position, it learns which other positions are relevant (the attention weights) and blends their representations accordingly. This enables massive parallelism during training and captures long-range dependencies without the vanishing gradient path lengths of RNNs.

**A brief history**: Neural networks were proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943. Rosenblatt's Perceptron (1958) was the first trainable single neuron. The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Minsky and Papert nearly killed the field by proving single-layer networks were limited. The backpropagation breakthrough came in 1986 (Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams). The 2012 AlexNet moment sparked the GPU-driven deep learning revolution. The 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' paper (Vaswani et al.) introduced the Transformer, which now dominates language and vision alike.

**Universal Approximation is not a free lunch.** The theorem says a sufficiently large neural network can approximate any continuous function — but it says nothing about how much data is needed to learn that approximation, how long training takes, or whether gradient descent will find it. In practice, depth and inductive biases (CNNs for images, attention for sequences) are essential. A theoretically sufficient network is often practically useless without the right architecture for the data structure.

**Common mistakes and interview insights:**

- **Forgetting to normalise inputs.** Raw pixel values 0–255 fed directly to a network cause wildly unequal gradient magnitudes. Always normalise inputs to mean 0, std 1 (or scale to [0,1]).
- **Using sigmoid in hidden layers.** Sigmoid saturates and causes vanishing gradients in deep networks. Default to ReLU in hidden layers; use sigmoid only at binary output.
- **Setting learning rate too high.** Loss bouncing or growing instead of shrinking = lr too large. Start with 1e-3 for Adam, 1e-2 for SGD.
- **Not shuffling training data.** Mini-batches drawn in order can introduce periodic correlations. Always shuffle between epochs.
- **Interview trap — 'why can't a deep linear network learn XOR?'** Because composing linear functions yields a linear function. The entire depth collapses to one weight matrix. Non-linearity is mandatory.
- **Interview trap — 'what happens if all weights are initialised to the same value?'** Symmetry breaking fails. Every neuron computes the same gradient and learns identically — you effectively have one neuron per layer. Random initialisation is essential.

items: A neuron computes `a = f(w · x + b)` — weighted sum of inputs plus bias, passed through a non-linear activation function. **Weights** set input importance; **bias** shifts the threshold; both are learned via gradient descent.

**Activation functions** (ReLU, sigmoid, softmax, tanh) introduce the non-linearity that allows stacked layers to approximate arbitrary functions. Without them, any depth of network collapses to a single linear transformation.

**Forward pass** propagates inputs layer-by-layer to produce predictions. **Backpropagation** applies the chain rule of calculus backward through the network to compute `dL/dW` for every parameter in O(n) time — this algorithmic efficiency is what makes deep learning practical at scale.

**Loss functions** (MSE for regression, binary cross-entropy for binary classification, categorical cross-entropy for multi-class) measure prediction error. They are paired with their natural output activations for clean gradients.

**Overfitting** is the central challenge: networks powerful enough to approximate any function are powerful enough to memorise noise. Dropout, L2 regularisation, early stopping, and batch normalisation are the main defences.

Beyond dense layers: **CNNs** use weight-sharing filters for spatial data; **RNNs/LSTMs** maintain hidden state for sequences; **Transformers** use attention to relate all positions simultaneously — underpinning GPT and BERT.

Deep learning's power is **hierarchical representation learning**: early layers detect low-level patterns (edges, phonemes), later layers combine them into abstract concepts (objects, words, intents), all learned end-to-end from labelled data without hand-crafted features.

quiz.question: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
options: The maximum of its input values
A weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function
The average of its input values multiplied by a scale factor
A random projection of its inputs into a higher-dimensional space
quiz.explanation: A neuron computes a = f(w · x + b). The dot product w · x is a weighted sum of inputs; b is a bias that shifts the activation threshold; f is the non-linear activation function. All three components are essential — the dot product for pattern matching, bias for positional flexibility, and activation for non-linearity.

quiz.question: Why are activation functions necessary in a multi-layer neural network?
options: They speed up matrix multiplication in hardware
They limit weights to a bounded range to prevent overflow
They introduce non-linearity so the network can learn non-linear functions; without them any depth collapses to one linear layer
They ensure outputs are always positive for numerical stability
quiz.explanation: Without non-linear activation functions, composing multiple linear layers (W2 · (W1 · x + b1) + b2) simplifies algebraically to a single equivalent linear transformation (W_combined · x + b_combined). Depth without non-linearity buys nothing. Activation functions are what enable deep networks to carve arbitrarily complex decision boundaries.

quiz.question: What is backpropagation, and what mathematical rule does it rely on?
options: An algorithm that initialises weights with small random values using probability theory
An algorithm that efficiently computes gradients of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule of calculus backward through the network
A forward pass variant that uses the quotient rule to estimate parameter sensitivity
An algorithm that passes predictions backward through layers to refine input representations
quiz.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule layer by layer, starting from the output loss and propagating gradient signals backward to each weight. It is O(n) in time — the same complexity as a forward pass — making it practical for networks with millions of parameters. Without it, computing gradients would require n separate forward passes (finite differences), which is infeasible at scale.

quiz.question: Which activation function is the recommended default for hidden layers in modern deep networks, and why?
options: Sigmoid — because it maps all inputs to a probability in (0,1)
Tanh — because it is zero-centered and always better than sigmoid
ReLU — because it is fast to compute and does not saturate for positive inputs, avoiding vanishing gradients
Softmax — because it normalises outputs across all neurons to sum to 1
quiz.explanation: ReLU (max(0,x)) passes its gradient through unchanged (gradient = 1) for positive inputs, avoiding the vanishing gradient problem that afflicts sigmoid and tanh when they saturate. It is also trivially fast to compute. Softmax is only for multi-class output layers; sigmoid for binary output; tanh for specific gating use cases like LSTMs.

quiz.question: Why can a network with no hidden layers (a single linear layer) not solve the XOR problem?
options: XOR requires floating-point precision that integer weights cannot provide
XOR is not linearly separable — no single hyperplane can divide its true outputs from its false outputs in input space
Linear layers cannot process boolean inputs; they require continuous values
A single layer has too few parameters to store the XOR truth table
quiz.explanation: XOR outputs 1 for (0,1) and (1,0), and 0 for (0,0) and (1,1). Plotting these in 2D, the 1s and 0s form an X pattern that cannot be separated by any straight line (hyperplane). A hidden layer introduces the non-linearity needed to create a curved or V-shaped decision boundary, solving the problem. This is the canonical proof that non-linearity matters.

quiz.question: What does the softmax activation function produce?
options: A single scalar value between -1 and 1 representing confidence
The index of the neuron with the highest pre-activation value
A probability distribution over classes where all values are positive and sum to 1
The raw unnormalised logit scores passed through a threshold function
quiz.explanation: Softmax computes exp(x_i) / Σ_j exp(x_j) for each element. The exponential ensures all values are positive, and dividing by the sum normalises them to sum to 1 — a valid probability distribution. Each output represents the model's estimated probability that the input belongs to that class. Used exclusively on multi-class output layers.

quiz.question: What does 'deep' mean in 'deep learning', and why does depth matter?
options: The model uses very large training datasets with deep coverage of examples
The network has many hidden layers, enabling hierarchical representation learning where each layer builds on the previous
The loss function is derived from deep mathematical theory such as information geometry
The model runs on specialised deep-memory hardware with many memory banks
quiz.explanation: 'Deep' refers to having multiple hidden layers. Depth enables hierarchical feature learning: early layers learn low-level features (edges, phonemes), middle layers combine them into mid-level patterns (textures, word parts), and later layers recognise high-level concepts (objects, intents). This learned hierarchy is far more efficient than a single wide layer for complex real-world data.

quiz.question: What is dropout regularisation, and when is it applied during the deep learning pipeline?
options: Removing weights below a threshold permanently during model pruning after training
Randomly zeroing a fraction of neuron activations during training to prevent over-reliance on individual neurons, disabled at inference
Stopping training early when validation loss stops improving over several epochs
Gradually reducing the learning rate to zero as training progresses toward convergence
quiz.explanation: Dropout randomly sets activations to zero with probability p (typically 0.2–0.5) during each training forward pass. This prevents neurons from co-adapting excessively and forces each to contribute robustly. At inference time dropout is disabled and weights are scaled by (1-p) to compensate. It acts as training an ensemble of 2^n sub-networks simultaneously.

quiz.question: What is the vanishing gradient problem and which activation function largely solves it for deep feedforward networks?
options: Gradients that grow too large during backprop, causing weight explosion; solved by sigmoid
Gradients that shrink exponentially toward zero as they propagate backward through many sigmoid or tanh layers; largely solved by ReLU
Loss values that vanish to zero after the first epoch; solved by using a larger learning rate
Weight updates that cancel out in symmetric networks; solved by random initialisation
quiz.explanation: Sigmoid and tanh derivatives peak at 0.25 and 1 respectively but approach 0 at saturation. In a 10-layer network, multiplying these small derivatives together gives a gradient approaching 0^10 ≈ 0 — early layers receive essentially no training signal. ReLU's gradient is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so it passes gradient signals backward unchanged, enabling training of networks with tens or hundreds of layers.

quiz.question: What is the key architectural difference between a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) layer and a dense (fully-connected) layer?
options: Dense layers use non-linear activations; convolutional layers use only linear operations
Convolutional layers share filter weights across all spatial positions, dramatically reducing parameters and exploiting local spatial structure
Convolutional layers can only process 1D input sequences, not 2D images
Dense layers are trained with backpropagation; convolutional layers require a separate training algorithm
quiz.explanation: A convolutional layer slides a small filter (e.g., 3×3) across the entire input, computing the same dot product at each position with the same weights — weight sharing. A 3×3 filter producing 32 feature maps has only 288 parameters regardless of input size. A dense layer connecting 28×28 pixels to 256 neurons has 200,704 parameters. Weight sharing also exploits translation equivariance: the same edge detector works everywhere in the image.
